(MarijuanaNews note: There are several things going on here.

First, on the most basic level we have a presentation of the Dutch prohibitionist position, and the Dutch government response. And yes, there are Dutch prohibitionists. Prohibitionists from other countries use these Dutch sources as authoritative: " Even the Dutch admit that their policy is a " failure. "

Second, as with the Canadian prohibitionists, the Dutch prohibitionists do not hesitate to misrepresent the situation in their own country and then ignore the much worse alternatives in other places. In this regard, prohibitionism is no different from other ideologies in commanding a loyalty above all else, especially the truth and logic. As is usually the case, this is another instance in which marijuana and the sale of marijuana are blamed for everything that is allegedly wrong with anything in Holland, except for the weather.

Third, the Dutch prohibitionist position comes to us courtesy of the Swedish prohibitionist propaganda site the Hassela Nordic Network, which is about as extreme as anything in the Western world. The Swedish prohibitionists are obsessed with the Dutch, but this is not just a bilateral affair. Marijuana prohibition is driven by an international ideology.

Fourth, we can see here the development of a prohibitionist line. When a new prohibitionist " product " is placed on the market, it is rapidly spread around the world and used as the " authoritative source " for other such pieces. The item below which appears to been a spin-off of last year’s Foreign Affairs prohibitionist triumph, but the most recent iteration has itself been echoed recently in Australia. And so it goes.

Unfortunately, the response is barely adequate, and even this would never have been seen by the rest of the world, if it were not for the efforts of a very distinguished retired Dutch diplomat who took the time to translate it.

I think that more needs to be done, hence the frequent focus on anti-Dutch prohibitionist propaganda on MarijuanaNews.

There is a lot here, but I think it is worth the time.)

" The failure of Dutch drug policy "

According to a programme, broadcast by the Dutch Netwerk-TV on March 12, it's obvious that there is increasing, domestic criticism of the Dutch drug policy.

This unique television programme is the first to 'allow' massive domestic criticism of what the advocates of a 'tolerant' drug policy have defined as " innovative and pragmatic. "

Having watched the programme and heard the comments by high-profile Dutch officials, the alleged success of the Dutch drug policy rather seems to be the result of uncontrolled tolerance in combination with lack of knowledge. Result: Holland's Half-Baked Drug Experiment.

In this release, HNN gives a summary of the facts and statements from the Dutch television programme.

In the programme, it's stated that Amsterdam, the No.1 Dutch tourist attraction, has 210 so-called coffee shops where cannabis products are freely available and 75 so-called hash-bars - establishments frequently visited by large number of drug tourists. Officials from the Netherlands are of the opinion that the country handles its drug policy in a 'mature' way and scientists and officials are even proud of the country's drug policy.

Peter Cohen from the University of Amsterdam thinks that tolerance is an excellent way of handling the drug problem, even if the future development is unknown. Cohen says tolerance keeps people away from prison and also alleviates (sic!) social problems.

(MarijuanaNews note: Peter Cohen is a good friend, and an outstanding scholar. There are two pieces of his work linked from the MarijuanaNews Go Dutch! page.)

Jaap de Vlieger, Head of the Rotterdam Police Drug Squad: I myself plead for: Stop that tolerance policy. It's the strangest thing we have, because it means that the problem is unmanageable. We really should stop that policy of tolerance.

C. Steinmetz: Yes, because they gradually discovered that all trails went via Holland - either direct via Holland, or via, let's say, via Dutch organisations working abroad.

It is said that ideologies have disappeared, that they no longer exist. But take a look at the discussion about the drug policy and you will certainly get the impression that facts and figures are apparently less important than ideology.

From the Dutch Parliament:

Parliamentary written QUESTIONS by Member of Parliament Van der Vlies of the SGP-Dutch Reformed political party (protestant, conservative) and ANSWERS by Mrs E. Borst-Eilers, Minister of Health, Welfare And Sports, also on behalf of the Minister of Justice, regarding NETHERLANDS DRUG POLICIES

The Hague, April 6th 1999
(unofficial translation by Jan van der Tas, member of the board of the Netherlands Drug Policy Foundation)
(MarijuanaNews note: Jan van der Tas is one of the most impressive people I have ever met. He is a retired Dutch diplomat. His last post was as the Netherland’s Ambassador to Germany, obviously a very important position for the Dutch.)

Q 1 Has the Minister taken note of the article published in the German newspaper 'Die Welt' on March 13th 2000, containing a report on a TV program broadcast by 'Netwerk' on March 12th 2000, under the title: " Drug Policy in the Netherlands Unsuccessful.

Devastating results after a 25-year field trial - Holland is a major trade center "?

A 1 Yes

Q 2 How does the Minister assess the statement made in this 'Netwerk' program by the American drugs researcher Larry Collins, according to which the Netherlands at the moment are supposed to be the largest producer of XTC.

How does this relate to the present policy with regard to XTC?
A 2 Already the Government Memorandum on Drugs policy of 1995 ( " Continuity and Change " ) mentions the fact that the Netherlands are seen as an important production country for XTC and XTC-like substances. Recent reports of the International Narcotics Control Board (INCB) contain indications of a world-wide growth in production and trade of synthetic drugs and in this context also the Netherlands are mentioned frequently.
The Netherlands Government considers this development with concern. Therefor in the last few years the Netherlands policies with regard to the fight against drug-related crime have been concentrated on combating trade in and production of synthetic drugs. This is shown by the establishment of the 'Unit Synthetic Drugs'. In the government's interim progress-reports on drug p olicy 1997 and 1999 parliament was informed about developments in this field. The INCB is also fully informed about this approach.

In its annual report 1999 INCB gives a balanced appreciation of the situation in the Netherlands. Although the Netherlands are still seen as one of the countries where most XTC and amphetamines are produced, the INCB shows esteem for the energy with which the Netherlands' police and judiciary have proceeded to dismantle laboratories as well as for the precision with which the Netherlands supply INCB with statistical data and information about exports of substances that can be used in the production of synthetic
drugs (so-called 'precursors').

Recently a Memorandum of Understanding was signed with Italy to further the fight against international trade in synthetic drugs and precursors. With France earlier arrangements had been made already in this sector of the fight against drugs.

Q 3 Is the Minister aware of recently published results of research done by the 'Trimbos-institute', according to which at least one percent of the Netherlands' youngsters consume heroin, four percent cocaine and eight percent regularly swallow amphetamine- and XTC-pills? By what measures does the minister intend to force back these horrific figures in the near future?
Q 4 Is it possible - on the basis of the data mentionned above - to come to the conclusion, that the use of hard drugs among Dutch youngsters of secondary school age is only exceeded by hard drug consumption of that age group in the United States? What is the Minister's answer to the allegations, according to which the Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sports " systematically ignore " these figures, as not fitting in with present drug policies, and that data emanating from independent research regarding the harmfulness of cannabis have been repeatedly swept under the carpet?

A 3&4 'Die Welt' and 'Netwerk' have wrongly given the impression as if these percentages refer to regular ('last 30 days') use of drugs among Dutch juveniles. As a matter of fact however, these figures refer to the so-called 'life-time prevalence' of use of certain drugs among 15/16 year olds, which means it includes all those who have at least one time in their whole life experimented with a particular drug. Evidently data which reflect actual, 'last 30 days' consumption, point at a considerably lower level of use.

The international comparison of life-time prevalence of drug use in the 15/16 year age group is taken from the Annual Report 1999 of the European Monitoring Centre for Drugs and Drug Addiction (EMCDDA).
See www.emcdda.org

For the Netherlands EMCDDA has used data from a school survey 1996 of the 'Trimbos-institute'. However, even these figures have been misinterpreted by the 'Netwerk' program. The EMCDDA report certainly does not allow the conclusion that life-time prevalence of hard drug use among the Dutch 15/16 years age group is surpassed only by the figures for the United States.

Thus the data show, that life-time prevalence of heroin consumption in Denmark, Ireland, Italy and the United Kingdom is higher than in the Netherlands. With regard to countries outside the EU, in the United States and Australia – for the last month -- higher percentages are measured for the consumption of heroin, cocaine and amphetamines than in the Netherlands. The Netherlands are however front runner in the EU regarding life-time prevalence of cocaine use among 15/16 year old secondary school pupils. Regarding XTC, in Ireland and the UK higher or comparable figures are measured in comparison with the Netherlands, and for amphetamines also the UK percentages are considerably higher.

Finally, it should be noted that these figures demonstrate, that it is particularly difficult to prove a relationship from cause to effect between drug use (both in the sense of life-time prevalence and in the sense of last month prevalence) and drug policies, like the 'Netwerk' program pretends to have established.

The 'Netwerk' allegation that the Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sports " systematically ignores " these figures is a factual misconception.

In the government's Progress report on Drug Policies (Sept 97 - Sept 99) various data on drug use are presented, among which the ones from the school survey 1996. In the First Annual Report National Drug Monitor the facts and figures, which both the 'Netwerk' program and the 'Die Welt' used unfairly, are presented and commented upon in a correct way.

The allegation according to which the Minister of Health, Welfare and Sports should repeatedly have swept independent research data about the harmfulness of cannabis under the carpet, can not be commented upon, for lack of any specification. The Minister is aware of no evidence that could substantiate such accusations.

As for the policies pursued, reference can be made to the recently presented Progress Report on Drug Policy 1997-1999, in which among other things the prevention-strategy of the Government is described. Use of drugs among school-age groups is discouraged by information and orientation specifically targeted at these groups.

A good example is the project developed by the 'Trimbos-institute' called 'The healthy school and stimulants', which is applied in many schools and has met with considerable interest in other EU-countries.

Q 5 Is the allegation correct, according to which in the last 25 years scarcely any systematic research into the effects of cannabis has taken places, as put forward in the 'Netwerk' program by Mr. Walburg, managing director of the Amsterdam based 'Jellinek-clinic' (for addiction-treatment)? Is the Minister willing to commission such research at short notice?

A 5 Mr Walburg's statement is patently incorrect. No (illegal) drug has been the object of so much research as cannabis. A simple search in MEDLINE (the data-base for international medical litterature) easily yields over 5000 articles that predominantly deal with medical, pharmacological and health aspects of cannabis use. On top of that MEDLINE gives links to 2700 articles that fall into the category human cannabis research. The World Health Organization in her 1997 report 'Cannabis: a health perspective and research agenda' has summarized the risks of cannabis use. Regarding research in the Netherlands as examples one can mention the extensive literature study on long term risks of long term cannabis use by the National Institute for Health and Environmental Hygiene, a study into the links between cannabis use and schizophrenia, a study into the effects of cannabis on driving performance by the University of Maastricht,
See
1994 Dutch Study On " Marijuana Use And Driving " In Real World Conditions
the study project regarding experienced cannabis users in Amsterdam and the comparative study now under way among experienced users in Amsterdam, Bremen and San Francisco.

Furthermore in the Netherlands studies are periodically undertaken with regard to prevalence of cannabis use, the THC content of cannabis on the market and the risks of pesticides on cannabis products.

Likewise reference must be made to the 'Addiction program' of 'ZON/NWO' (institutes for fundamental research in nature and the natural sciences) in the framework of which it is the scientific community and the addiction care institutes (the Jellinek institute among them) who, to an important degree, themselves can fill in the priorities for studies and projects. In the context of this program in the last year virtually no single proposal for research into the effects of cannabis has been submitted.

The impression created by the 'Netwerk' program, according to which the Ministry would actively oppose such research, is blatantly at odds with the truth.

Q 6 What is your answer to the judgment put forward in the 'Netwerk' program, according to which the Netherlands, in spite of the drug policies pursued, has no fewer hard drug users than other countries and has become a prominent trading centre for drugs. How does the minister evaluate the finding by 'Netwerk' that nobody in the world takes the Netherlands' 'drugs-experiment' seriously?

A 6 Reference can be made to the answers to questions 2, 3, and 4. The fight against trade and production enjoys a high priority in Dutch drug policies, and, judging from the results obtained (among other things the large quantities of drugs confiscated), is effective. On the basis of the data presented by 'Netwerk' with regard to 'life-time prevalence' of drug use among 15/16 year old secondary school pupils, no verdict is possible about the level of regular (last month prevalence) drug use among the total population.

Furthermore, correct data about the number of addicts or problematic users respectively in the EU, indicate that the Netherlands have fewer addicts than Belgium, Denmark, Ireland, France, Italy, Luxemburg and the United Kingdom (EMCDDA, Annual Report 1999).

The finding that nobody in the world takes the Netherlands' 'drugs experiment' serious, must be contradicted. More and more member-states of the EU are taking measures in the field of 'harm-reduction ". This concept, ever since the seventies, has been at the root of Netherlands' drug policies. In practice this leads to measures like needle exchange, methadone treatment and low threshold care facilities. Only a few years ago, the Netherlands were fiercely criticized by many countries, for pursuing these policies. Where cannabis is concerned, the recent annual report of the EMCDDA shows clearly, that more and more countries de facto apply a tolerance regime with regard to the individual user.

Besides, from the many bilateral contacts between Dutch and foreign experts and policy-makers, it becomes evident that Dutch policies now meet with a high degree of appreciation. It therefor remains obscure on what factual data the 'Netwerk' findings are based.
